A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–B are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic motion and toy-model experiments, ImageNet activation interventions, and ISIC debiasing results, with supplementary analyses in Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds transformer evaluations, layer-wise analyses, prediction-intervention tests, and further debiasing and intervention results.

M1.justification: Non-target attribution, activation-minimizing feature visualization, and the presence-plus-absence debiasing losses remain unchanged. V2 experimentally implements the attribution-subset selection strategy already suggested in v1 Section 6; this does not establish a new method component.

E1.justification: The synthetic motion, colored-pixel, ImageNet-1k, and ISIC tasks remain. Appendix B.4 adds an ISIC scenario described as having weaker spurious correlations. The added ViT evaluations extend model configurations rather than introducing another dataset or task.

E2.justification: The most-activating-patch control already appeared at the default CNN setting in v1 Appendix B.3. V2 extends it across the existing hyperparameter comparisons in Table 3 and displays it in Table 1. Logical-NOT and debiasing comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds substantial evaluation protocols: ViT-B/16 measurements using minimum activation over tokens, earlier-layer measurements, prediction-flip tests with a suppression-only control, and attribution evaluation on selected ten-image subsets. It also introduces weaker-bias training and quantitative controlled-versus-patch interventions. These supplement the retained original protocols.

E4.justification: New analyses test where inhibition occurs across layers, whether it affects ImageNet predictions independently of increased activations, whether selective attribution computation remains informative, and whether debiasing survives weaker correlations. Appendix B.5 adds quantitative validation of patch interventions against data-generation-based interventions; v1 had only the qualitative controlled-intervention examples.

E5.justification: V2 adds standard deviations for the previously reported most-activating-patch control. However, Appendix B.3 removes the explicit SciPy independent t-test description and aggregate CNN p-values while retaining significant-channel counts. The existing five-run disclosures and other standard-deviation reporting remain.

E6.justification: V2 adds ViT, layer-wise, prediction-flip, attribution-subset, weaker-bias, and quantitative intervention results. Examples include suppression-only flip rates of 8.2% versus 3.5% for random patches, and weaker-bias inverse accuracies of 0.64 versus 0.46 for presence-only debiasing. Figure 4 also changes activation labels, including 2.9 to 3.2 and -7 to -6.9. Original CNN Table 1 and ISIC Table 2 scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Sections 2.1 and A.2 newly specify the concept underlying the formal definition as a family of input patterns sharing a neuronal effect, explicitly excluding semantic coherence as a formal requirement. The encoded-absence inequalities, constructive existence argument, feature-direction definition, and loss equations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about encoded absences, limitations of standard explanations, complementary explanation methods, and absence-aware debiasing. Additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for layer-dependent inhibition and qualifications about measurements before residual addition in Appendix B.3. Appendices A.4–A.5 discuss transformer applicability and positive-potential stability under sparse inputs. It also clarifies the distinction between formal pattern families and semantic interpretations, while retaining the earlier intervention-approximation caveat.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code repository address on the first page and technical information for the new experiments, including token aggregation, measured layer locations, InputXGradient channel selection, and eight-patch and ten-image selection procedures. Existing training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 3 adds positioning against concept-discovery approaches, including WWW and CLIP-Dissect. New references also support the ViT, GeLU, and Swish discussions. The Walter et al. reference changes title and publication information while retaining its role in the argument.

P1.justification: V2 adds localized explanatory paragraphs and appendix subsections, including A.5, while preserving the main section sequence and most existing prose. Author-affiliation and publication text are updated. This is an expansion within the existing narrative structure rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a ViT column and most-activating row; Table 3 gains a control column. New Tables 4, 6, and 7 present supplementary analyses using the existing visual style. Existing figures are largely preserved with reflow, and v1 Table 4 becomes v2 Table 5.

improvement.justification: V1's ImageNet evidence centered on neuron activations, and its controlled-intervention check was qualitative. V2 adds a suppression-only prediction test and quantitative controlled-versus-patch comparisons, substantially strengthening the links to decisions and intervention validity. ViT and weaker-bias experiments further support generality. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit t-test details, although the new suppression-only procedure remains briefly specified.
